text: In December 1952, Londoners walked into movie theaters only to find the screen completely invisible—because the smog had seeped inside the building.
Within five days, four thousand citizens were dead. But this wasn't an enemy wartime chemical attack. It was ordinary living room fireplace smoke.
A freak atmospheric inversion trapped a layer of freezing air over the Thames valley. A warm ceiling sat at two hundred meters, locking all smoke beneath it like a glass lid.
Every day, London burned thousands of tons of high-sulfur coal. Inside the dense fog droplets, sulfur dioxide reacted with nitrogen, catalyzing into airborne sulfuric acid.
When the government plotted air samples against morgue intake, the curves matched in absolute lockstep. As sulfur levels peaked, daily deaths quadrupled.
The deadly yellow fog forced Parliament to ban smoky fuels in cities forever, giving birth to the modern environmental movement.
